summary: 14-day analysis shows overall Time in Range of 86% with notable hypoglycemia (TBR 5.1%), especially overnight. Daytime patterns reveal post-prandial hyperglycemia likely due to unannounced meals, followed by delayed insulin-induced lows. The primary actionable finding is nocturnal basal oversupply. Automation settings are generally appropriate but the max IOB limit is set too high, posing stacking risk. No meal logging prevents assessment of carb ratios, ISF, or DIA; logging meals is essential for further optimization.

analysis_steps.findings: CGM coverage 98.7%, cadence 5 minutes. 10 gaps (largest 65 minutes). No invalid or duplicate entries. Profile has all 23 decision-inventory parameters. Telemetry includes glucose, treatments, device statuses, and loop logs. Comprehensive for basal and oxygen-level analysis.
analysis_steps.evidence: data_quality section of telemetry, counts, coverage_percent, gap_count.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No gaps that block basal and safety analysis, but missing carbohydrate entries limit meal-related insights.

analysis_steps.findings: Overall TIR 86%, TBR 5.1%, TAR 8.9%. Hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL) on multiple days with lows down to 41 mg/dL. Overnight lows most pronounced. Hyperglycemia peaks in afternoon (hourly averages up to 162 mg/dL, TAR up to 32%). CV 32.6%. Correction doses often followed by large drops. A pump error (occlusion) noted on Aug 19.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: Absence of meal logs prevents distinguishing meal-driven highs from basal deficit.

analysis_steps.findings: Overnight hours 0–2 show average glucose 91–102 mg/dL but TBR 11–18% and minimums to 54 mg/dL, indicating basal oversupply relative to the 90 mg/dL target. Frequent 0 U/h temp basals confirm the system compensating. Daytime basal segments (0.5–0.8 U/h) appear in line with glucose trends but cannot be fully isolated from meals. Targets (90/100/90 mg/dL) are appropriate.
analysis_steps.evidence: hourly_glucose_local, basal_segments, target_segments, representative_treatments (temp basals), daily_glucose.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carbohydrate entries to separate meal contributions from basal adequacy during daytime.

analysis_steps.findings: Carb ratios (10.5–13.2 g/U) cannot be assessed without meal data. ISF of 56 mg/dL/U appears aggressive; correction boluses often cause drops >100 mg/dL. DIA of 10 h likely contributes to insulin stacking and late post-correction hypoglycemia. Dynamic ISF further amplifies effective sensitivity. No direct evidence for specific CR or ISF changes.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: Missing meal entries block evaluation of CR and meal-related ISF; only correction responses observed.

analysis_steps.findings: SMB and UAM both enabled; SMB always active. Settings (3 min interval, 15 min SMB-basal-minutes, 20 min UAM-basal-minutes) are appropriate for current low basal rates. The system frequently suspends (0 U/h) to prevent lows, confirming it is compensating for basal excess rather than causing hypoglycemia. Activation conditions safe.
analysis_steps.evidence: aaps_profile.smb_settings, representative_treatments, loop statuses showing 0 U/h temp basals triggered by low predictions.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: Without meal announcements, UAM contribution to insulin delivery cannot be quantified.

analysis_steps.findings: Max IOB 25 U and max basal 12 U/h far exceed actual needs (typical daily insulin ~20 U, peak IOB 5.9 U). These high safety limits allow stacking risk after multiple corrections. Dynamic ISF adjustment (70%) reduces effective ISF during rises, potentiating correction doses. Automation is not the root cause of lows but can exaggerate them if basal/ISF are too aggressive.
analysis_steps.evidence: aaps_profile.smb_settings.raw_settings (max_iob_units, max_basal_u_per_hour, dynamic_sensitivity_enabled, dynamic_isf_adjustment_factor_percent), therapy_response_windows, loop statuses (IOB, variable_sens).
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No meal data to isolate the role of manual bolus ISF vs. dynamic ISF.

analysis_steps.findings: Zero carb entries recorded. All insulin delivery for meals relies on UAM/SMB, causing delayed coverage with post-prandial hyperglycemia and later hypoglycemia. No meal-based bolus strategy can be recommended until the user starts logging meals with carbohydrate estimates.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: Complete absence of carbohydrate logging blocks any assessment.

analysis_steps.findings: No extended carb entries in telemetry and no e-carb declarations in profile. Without regular meal logs, absorption patterns cannot be inferred. Current carb absorption model settings are kept unchanged.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No carb data of any kind.

analysis_steps.findings: Primary issue: nocturnal hypoglycemia is driven by basal oversupply in the 00:00–05:00 segment (0.6 U/h). Frequent zero-temp basals confirm the excess. Secondary safety risk: max IOB limit of 25 U is excessive; observed IOB peaks at 5.9 U, so lowering to 8 U adds protection without restricting therapy. The ISF of 56 mg/dL/U appears aggressive but requires meal data for validation; DIA of 10 h may contribute to stacking but is not falsifiable without meal logs. Meal strategy is entirely blocked; logging all meals is the next essential step. All other settings, including CR, targets, and most automation parameters, are kept unchanged pending further data.
analysis_steps.evidence: Synthesis of all previous stages and checkpoints.
analysis_steps.data_gaps: No meal logs prevent full profile optimization; once meals are logged, ISF, DIA, and CR can be reassessed.

strengths: Good overall Time in Range (86%) and reliable CGM data quality.
Loop automation frequently intervenes with 0 U/h temp basals to protect against hypoglycemia.
Profile is well-structured with appropriate target ranges.
issues: Nocturnal hypoglycemia with readings down to 41 mg/dL, suggesting basal oversupply.
Max IOB safety limit (25 U) is set far above actual insulin needs, posing insulin stacking risk.
All meals are unannounced; this forces UAM-mediated coverage leading to post-prandial hyperglycemia followed by delayed hypoglycemia.
Correction boluses often result in excessive glucose drops, possibly due to aggressive ISF and long DIA.

recommendations.title: Reduce overnight basal from 00:00 to 05:00
recommendations.description: Nightly lows in the first half of the night indicate basal is too high. Reduce the basal rate from 0.6 U/h to 0.5 U/h during the 00:00–05:00 segment to lower hypoglycemia risk.

recommendations.title: Lower max IOB safety limit
recommendations.description: The current max IOB of 25 U is effectively unlimited. Observed IOB reaches 5.9 U. Reducing to 8 U adds a safety guard without restricting typical insulin needs.

recommendations.title: Start logging all meals with carbohydrate estimates
recommendations.description: Without meal announcements, the system cannot provide timely boluses. Logging meals will enable CR, ISF, and DIA evaluation, reduce post-prandial highs, and lower delayed hypoglycemia risk.

profile_recommendation.recommendation: Reduce the basal rate from 00:00 to 05:00 from 0.6 U/h to 0.5 U/h.
profile_recommendation.rationale: Hourly local glucose data show frequent lows and high time-below-range in the early night hours. The automation repeatedly sets 0 U/h temp basals, confirming insulin surplus. A 0.1 U/h reduction is a safe first step to mitigate nocturnal hypoglycemia without causing major hyperglycemia.
profile_recommendation.next_check: Monitor overnight glucose for three nights after the change. If lows persist, consider further reduction or evaluate other factors such as DIA or evening bolus strategies.

meal_strategy_summary.suggestion: No prebolus or immediate bolus percentage can be recommended because no meals have been logged. Start logging all meals with estimated carbohydrate grams. For now, continue using SMB/UAM for coverage, but be aware that unannounced meals cause delayed insulin delivery, leading to post-meal highs and later lows. Once meal data are available, evaluate the need for prebolus timing and immediate bolus percentage.
meal_strategy_summary.rationale: All current meal coverage relies on UAM, which reacts to rising glucose rather than anticipating it. This results in a consistent pattern of post-prandial hyperglycemia in the afternoon and evening, followed by insulin stacking and hypoglycemia. Logging meals will enable proactive delivery and reduce volatility.
meal_strategy_summary.next_observation: Collect at least 3 days of meal logs with carbohydrate estimates, then re-analyze post-prandial excursions to assess CR and prebolus needs.

implementation_steps: 1. Discuss the proposed basal rate reduction (00:00–05:00 from 0.6 to 0.5 U/h) with your healthcare provider. Implement the change one night at a time, monitoring overnight glucose closely for the next three nights.
2. After confirming that overnight lows are reduced, adjust the max IOB safety limit to 8 U to prevent insulin stacking.
3. Begin logging all meals with approximate carbohydrate amounts. This is essential for future optimization of carb ratios, ISF, and DIA.
4. After collecting at least three days of meal logs and stable nocturnal patterns, re-evaluate CR, ISF, and DIA settings with your care team.
education: Unannounced meals force the system to rely on reactive UAM insulin delivery, causing a delay that leads to post-meal hyperglycemia and later hypoglycemia when insulin accumulates.
A long DIA (Duration of Insulin Action) of 10 hours means that correction and meal boluses can stack over many hours, increasing the risk of overnight lows if basal is too high or ISF is aggressive.
Reducing overnight basal is often the safest first adjustment to address nocturnal lows without affecting daytime coverage.
safety_notes: This is decision-support content only. Verify each proposed change independently, make one change at a time, and monitor glucose closely.
Always consult with your healthcare team before adjusting insulin therapy.
After lowering basal, watch for unexpected hyperglycemia in the following days as an indication of insufficient basal.
